source.title: PROC-STRATEGY-001: optimize ex-ante flexible and backup capacity commitments
source.body:
## Purpose

Build the first-stage decision layer above [#5099 static portfolio sourcing](https://github.com/Luminous-Dynamics/mycelix/pull/5099) and [#5108 adaptive recourse](https://github.com/Luminous-Dynamics/mycelix/pull/5108): choose which flexible/backup options to pre-commit, and how much reserved capacity to purchase, before disruption occurs.

This is a research/reference optimization task. It is not contract execution, supplier outreach, spend authorization, or a live purchasing system.

## Architecture split

- **Static portfolio layer (#5099):** chooses a normal/base supplier allocation.
- **Recourse layer (#5108):** given a fixed baseline and a fixed set of already-committed options, computes scenario-specific on-time recovery under explicit constraints.
- **This issue:** selects the option set/capacity before scenarios are realized, then evaluates the same committed plan across the frozen scenario set using #5108 semantics.

Keep these layers separable for differential tests; first-stage selection must not call a live authority or treat scenario probabilities as known by default.

## Paradigm shift

Move from "buy a backup supplier" to "price the option value of flexible capacity and standby recovery." An option is valuable only when its capacity, qualification, activation lead, transit time, common-cause dependencies, fees and scenario coverage make recovery feasible.

## Required decision variables and constraints

- Which pre-qualified flexible/backup options to commit.
- How much capacity to reserve per option, respecting minimums/increments and shared capacity-pool ceilings.
- Upfront retainer/option fees, activation fees, unit costs and transport costs.
- Baseline allocation + reserved contingency capacity must respect capacity accounting without double pledging the same pool.
- Minimum service-level target (optional, versioned) and total budget.
- Scenario-by-scenario feasible recourse and on-time recovery; no supplier capacity may be activated twice across conflicting commitments.
- Failure-domain overlap across supplier parent, plant, critical sub-tier, utility, route, port and geography.
- Exact evidence freshness, qualification, quote and option validity.

## Optimization semantics

Initially, use a bounded exact first-stage enumerator for very small cases. Evaluate each candidate commitment set by invoking an independently implemented second-stage recourse oracle—not by asking a candidate set to score itself. Compare strategies across cost, worst-case shortage, scenario-level shortage distribution and coverage.

If disruption probabilities are uncalibrated, use declared scenarios and worst-case envelopes rather than expected-cost claims. If a probability model is later admitted, bind its source, training/calibration window, version, uncertainty set and out-of-sample qualification evidence.

Do not force all trade-offs into an unversioned scalar. A policy may apply explicit feasibility constraints and a declared lexicographic objective, or present a Pareto frontier for authorized human/policy selection.

## Required baselines

1. No flexible/backup capacity.
2. Cheapest backup-only contract.
3. Flexible-only contract.
4. Backup-only contract.
5. Greedy “reserve the cheapest capacity first.”
6. Exhaustive joint first-/second-stage optimum on tractable cases.

Every strategy uses the exact same frozen input and scenario manifest.

## Independent verifier and adversarial cases

- Capacity promised to normal supply is also sold as backup.
- Multiple offer IDs share one capacity pool or supplier parent.
- Flexible/backup capacity exists but activation plus transit misses the deadline.
- Option fee is sunk even when the option is unused.
- A reserve is already committed to another request.
- A backup supplier is hit by the same plant/port/utility/sub-tier disruption as the base source.
- Quote, qualification, or capacity evidence expires before scenario execution.
- Model chooses a cheap option but exceeds total budget after activation fees.
- A generated scenario is accidentally treated as a calibrated probability.
- Search bounds are exceeded but a partial plan is labelled optimal.
- Candidate order changes an exact tie.
- An option set meets nominal demand but fails all severe disruption cases.

## Proposed benchmarks (not measured)

- Exact agreement with independent exhaustive oracle for every tractable first-stage/recourse instance.
- Zero shared-capacity overcommitment, invalid option activation, deadline violation or budget breach.
- 100% report of baseline costs, reserved capacity, option fees, activated quantities, scenario-level recourse cost and shortage.
- Report cost regret versus the exact optimum on tractable instances and gap/unknown status on larger instances.
- At least 10,000 generated micro-instances after the first independent oracle passes.
- Measure p50/p95/max runtime and memory on named pinned hardware before setting performance promises.

## Research references

- Dai, Zou & Zhang (2026), robust supplier selection/order allocation using normal, flexible and backup modes: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijpe.2026.110060
- Li, Doan & Branke (online 2026/preprint), distributionally robust sourcing under uncertain disruption impact: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijpe.2026.110160
- Hosseini et al. (2019), reactive restoration and disruption dependencies: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijpe.2019.03.018

These papers motivate comparable experiments; reported gains are not expected results for Mycelix.

## Claim ceiling

No live supplier contact, purchase orders, contract amendments, inventory mutations, payment execution, dispatch or legal-conformity claim. Start with synthetic civilian maintenance supplies, repairable IT equipment, food essentials and community infrastructure.
